paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can learn inefficiently or develop unwanted behavior when its reward does not properly express the intended task. This paper proposes symbolic reward machines as a way to combine high-level task knowledge with reward learning. They extend reward machines by allowing their transitions to contain predicates and symbolic reward outputs.

The symbolic values leave parts of the reward specification to be inferred from demonstrations. The central problem is assigning those values using only a few examples of expert behavior. The authors develop a hierarchical Bayesian approach that seeks likely assignments under which the completed reward machine distinguishes expert trajectories from other trajectories with high accuracy.

This approach gives task structure and demonstrations complementary roles: the structure expresses high-level knowledge, while demonstrations help determine its concrete reward values. Experiments show that the learned machines can substantially improve training efficiency on complex reinforcement learning tasks and generalize across different environment configurations. These results support learning rewards within a structured representation rather than specifying every reward value manually.
icml-2022-a-hierarchical-bayesian-approa.tldr: Symbolic reward machines combine task knowledge with Bayesian inference from a few expert demonstrations to learn rewards that improve reinforcement learning efficiency.

paragraphs: Natural language models can be vulnerable to deliberately modified inputs. This paper approaches that vulnerability through causal reasoning and introduces Causal Intervention by Semantic Smoothing, or CISS. The framework aims to learn the effect of intervening on an input, expressed as p(y|do(x)), rather than relying solely on associations in observed examples.

CISS performs smoothing in a latent semantic space, where text is represented in terms of learned meaning. This supplies the mechanism for making robust predictions. The authors describe the framework as scalable to deep architectures and as avoiding the need to construct a separate, customized noise process for each particular attack.

The paper provides a robustness proof for word substitution attacks and empirical evidence under stronger perturbations involving previously unknown attack algorithms. On YELP, it reports a 6.8% advantage over the runner-up in certified robustness to word substitutions and 80.7% empirical robustness when syntactic attacks are included. The distinction matters: the word substitution result has a formal guarantee, while the broader attack result is supported by experiments.
icml-2022-certified-robustness-against-n.tldr: CISS uses causal intervention through semantic smoothing to provide certified robustness to word substitutions and empirical robustness to broader language attacks.

paragraphs: Comparing two collections of text can require reading many examples before a meaningful pattern becomes clear. This paper turns that work into a language generation problem: find a description that applies more frequently to one collection than the other. The desired output is an understandable hypothesis about the difference between the distributions.

The system first uses a fine-tuned GPT-3 model to propose descriptions from samples of both collections. A learned verifier then checks the candidates against a larger set of samples and reorders them according to the evidence. Generation supplies possible explanations, while verification tests whether those explanations describe a broader pattern beyond the initial examples.

Across 54 real-world binary classification tasks, GPT-3 Curie produces descriptions similar to human annotations 7% of the time without the proposed improvements, rising to 61% with fine-tuning and reranking. The best Davinci-based system reaches 76%. The authors also use the generated descriptions to examine distribution shifts, identify dataset shortcuts, summarize unknown tasks, and name text clusters, demonstrating several uses for readable comparisons.
icml-2022-describing-differences-between.tldr: A language model proposes explanations of differences between text collections, and a learned verifier reranks them using evidence from additional samples.

paragraphs: The paper studies nonconvex optimization problems whose objective is a sum of individual functions. Its goal is to find a first-order stationary point, where the gradient is sufficiently small. Existing stochastic methods using higher-order derivatives had complexity bounds that depended on the number of dimensions, even when that dependence was only polylogarithmic.

The authors show that this dimension dependence is avoidable under the standard regularity setting considered. They introduce stochastic algorithms with new estimators for both first-order and higher-order derivatives. Given access to derivatives of order p, their method reaches an epsilon-stationary point using O(n^((2p-1)/(2p))/epsilon^((p+1)/p)) high-order oracle calls, where n counts the component functions.

The result improves two aspects of previous guarantees: dependence on n compared with existing deterministic higher-order methods, and dependence on dimension compared with stochastic higher-order methods. The contribution concerns the number of derivative-oracle calls required to meet a stationarity target. It establishes that the dimension factor in earlier bounds is not an essential obstacle for this class of algorithms.
icml-2022-dimension-free-complexity-boun.tldr: New stochastic derivative estimators yield dimension-free oracle complexity bounds for finding stationary points in nonconvex finite-sum optimization.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decision-making when losses can change adversarially but the environment's transition rules are known. It evaluates learning through dynamic regret: the performance difference between the learner and a sequence of feasible policies that may change over time. This benchmark permits the comparison policy to adapt as conditions change.

Dynamic regret is therefore a strictly stronger measure than static regret, which compares the learner with one fixed policy. The authors consider three settings: episodic stochastic shortest-path problems without loops, general episodic stochastic shortest-path problems, and infinite-horizon Markov decision processes. These cover different ways that decisions and their consequences can extend through time.

For each setting, the paper develops an online ensemble algorithm and proves a corresponding dynamic regret guarantee. The episodic shortest-path results, including the loop-free case, are minimax optimal in their dependence on the time horizon and a specified measure of nonstationarity. That optimality concerns these particular dependencies; the broader contribution is a set of guarantees that explicitly account for changing comparison policies.
icml-2022-dynamic-regret-of-online-marko.tldr: Online ensemble algorithms obtain dynamic regret guarantees for three MDP settings with known transitions and adversarially changing losses.

paragraphs: Strong board-game agents often require enormous amounts of self-play. This paper asks how to improve learning when the number of games is limited, building on AlphaZero to create PCZero. Its central addition is path consistency: the stated optimality principle that values along a single optimal search path should agree.

PCZero uses this principle to regularize path searching. Its implementation combines historical trajectories with paths explored through Monte Carlo tree search, aiming to balance exploration and exploitation and improve generalization. This connects learning signals across a search path, making consistency among its value estimates part of how the model learns.

On 13-by-13 Hex, PCZero achieves a 94.1% win rate against the 2015 Hex Computer Olympiad champion, compared with 84.3% for AlphaZero. The models use 900,000 self-play games, which the authors frame as an amount a human could study over a lifetime. Improvements also extend to Othello and Gomoku, and experiments support efficiency in an offline learning setting. These findings indicate gains from the path-consistency principle across the tested games and learning settings.
icml-2022-efficient-learning-for-alphaze.tldr: PCZero adds path-consistency regularization to AlphaZero, improving performance in tested board games under a limited self-play budget.

paragraphs: Forecasting becomes harder as predictions extend further into the future. This paper identifies two problems with Transformer-based forecasting: substantial computational cost and difficulty capturing a time series' overall profile, such as its trend. FEDformer addresses both by combining seasonal-trend decomposition with a Transformer that also works with frequency information.

The decomposition handles the broad structure of the series, while the Transformer captures finer details. The frequency component uses the observation that many time series have sparse representations in bases such as the Fourier basis. This gives the model another way to represent temporal structure while supporting complexity that grows linearly with sequence length.

Experiments on six benchmark datasets report prediction-error reductions of 14.8% for multivariate forecasting and 22.6% for univariate forecasting relative to state-of-the-art methods. The results support combining an explicit representation of broad temporal patterns with learned detailed structure. The reported efficiency and accuracy gains apply to the proposed architecture and evaluations, while the frequency design is motivated by sparsity that many, rather than all, time series exhibit.
icml-2022-fedformer-frequency-enhanced-d.tldr: FEDformer combines seasonal-trend decomposition and frequency-enhanced Transformers to improve long-term forecasting with linear sequence-length complexity.

paragraphs: This paper considers how to estimate a good maximizer of an unknown function from noisy examples. Instead of fitting an unrestricted predictor and then conducting a difficult search over it, the authors propose global optimization networks, or GONs. These fitted functions have a structure that makes their unique global maximizer easy to recover.

A GON composes an invertible function with a unimodal function. Its maximizer can be inferred in O(D) time, where D is the dimension, and then used as an estimate for the original black-box problem. The paper also develops lattice models with linear inequality constraints for specifying multidimensional unimodal functions and extends the approach to maximization conditional on selected inputs.

Experiments find that GON maximizers are statistically significantly better predictions than those obtained from convex fits, Gaussian process regression, or deep neural networks, and are more reasonable for the real-world problems studied. The structural guarantee concerns the fitted GON's maximizer; its usefulness for the unknown function is assessed empirically. This separates efficient optimization of the learned representation from the statistical task of estimating where the original function is best.
icml-2022-global-optimization-networks-3.tldr: Global optimization networks fit noisy function observations with a structured model whose unique maximizer can be recovered in linear time in dimension.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning requires adapting to a task from a small collection of support examples. HyperTransformer tackles this by using a Transformer to generate the weights of a convolutional neural network directly from those examples. The method covers both supervised and semi-supervised versions of the problem, making model generation the means of task adaptation.

The design separates the capacity needed to understand many possible tasks from the capacity needed to solve any one task. A large Transformer represents the relationship between support examples and model parameters, while the generated CNN can remain small. The paper finds this particularly effective for small CNNs, where letting task information influence all parameters performs better than relying on a fixed, task-independent embedding.

For larger target networks, the authors find that generating only the final layer can already match or improve on state-of-the-art results. This variant also remains differentiable from end to end. Together, the findings show that task-conditioned weight generation can be useful at different model sizes, with the appropriate extent of parameter generation changing between the small and larger architectures studied.
icml-2022-hypertransformer-model-generat.tldr: HyperTransformer generates task-specific CNN weights from a few support examples, allowing compact models to adapt throughout their parameters.

paragraphs: Learning differential equations from long sequences can make numerical integration slow and unstable. This paper changes how the dynamics are represented. It treats the target system as a vector field connected to a simpler base vector field through a differentiable, invertible transformation represented by an invertible neural network.

The method learns both the transformation and the dynamics of the base ordinary differential equation. This lets the neural network carry part of the complexity that would otherwise have to appear directly in the dynamics. By restricting the base equation to a form that is amenable to integration, the approach can make trajectory computation faster and more robust.

The authors evaluate the method on benchmark differential-equation systems and within continuous-depth neural networks, examining both training and evaluation. They report integration speedups of up to two orders of magnitude for learned equations. The mechanism behind the approach is the division of work between an integrable base system and a learned change of coordinates, with the reported speedup representing the upper end of the demonstrated results.
icml-2022-learning-efficient-and-robust-.tldr: An invertible neural network transforms an easy-to-integrate base ODE into richer learned dynamics, enabling reported integration speedups of up to 100-fold.

paragraphs: Link prediction estimates which connections are missing from a graph. Existing approaches commonly learn associations between observed graph structure and whether two nodes are connected. This paper adds a causal perspective by asking whether a connection would still exist under a different graph structure, using the resulting counterfactual links as additional training information.

The proposed causal model assigns distinct roles to the available information. Learned representations of node pairs provide context, global structural properties of the graph serve as the treatment, and link existence is the outcome. This formulation gives the method a way to create counterfactual examples about connections under altered structural conditions.

The prediction method then learns representations from both observed and generated counterfactual links. Its contribution is therefore a data augmentation strategy that incorporates the causal model into graph representation learning. Benchmark experiments report state-of-the-art link prediction performance. Those findings support the usefulness of the augmented training data for prediction in the tested settings, with the counterfactual links supplied by the proposed modeling framework.
icml-2022-learning-from-counterfactual-l.tldr: A causal data augmentation method generates counterfactual links and combines them with observed links to improve graph link prediction.

paragraphs: Simulating a physical system starts with its conditions and parameters and predicts what happens next. This paper studies the reverse task: recovering initial conditions or physical parameters from a sparse set of measurements. The recovered quantities must be considered within dynamics governed by a partial differential equation, making this a PDE-constrained inverse problem.

The authors combine graph neural networks with autodecoder-style priors to solve these problems. The graph network provides a learned approach to representing the physical dynamics, while the prior contributes structure to the recovery task. This extends the use of graph networks beyond forward simulation to inferring the unknown quantities that explain observed behavior.

In applications involving the wave equation and Navier–Stokes equations, the combined method estimates initial conditions or physical parameters more accurately than other learned approaches. The paper also reports computational speedups of up to 90-fold compared with principled solvers. These are two distinct findings: improved recovery accuracy relative to learned alternatives and faster computation relative to principled numerical approaches in the demonstrated tasks.
icml-2022-learning-to-solve-pde-constrai.tldr: Graph neural networks with autodecoder-style priors recover PDE initial conditions or parameters from sparse measurements, with improved accuracy and reported speedups up to 90-fold.

paragraphs: Random-feature attention approximates softmax attention while reducing time and memory requirements to linear complexity. This paper examines why that approximation is biased by interpreting it as self-normalized importance sampling. The interpretation connects the attention approximation to a statistical estimation problem and guides the design of alternative estimators.

The authors first introduce randomized attention, or RA, an unbiased estimator of the complete softmax attention operation. RA constructs positive random features from distributions tailored to individual queries, substantially improving approximation fidelity. Its cost remains quadratic, however, so the more faithful estimator alone does not retain the efficiency advantage of conventional random-feature attention.

The paper then develops linear randomized attention, or LARA, combining RA's expressive approach with the efficiency of random-feature attention. LARA has linear complexity, while the unbiasedness claim in the abstract specifically belongs to RA. Experiments across multiple domains show substantial performance improvements over random-feature attention for both methods. The contribution thus connects an explanation of approximation bias to a more accurate estimator and a separate efficient attention mechanism.
icml-2022-linear-complexity-randomized-s.tldr: A sampling-based analysis leads to unbiased randomized attention and to LARA, a linear-complexity mechanism that improves on random-feature attention.

paragraphs: Methods intended to improve generalization under distribution shifts can themselves overfit when used with large, overparameterized models. This paper focuses on that difficulty for distributionally robust optimization and invariant risk minimization. It proposes MAPLE, which changes the importance assigned to training examples so that ordinary weighted training produces better out-of-distribution performance.

The key mechanism is a bilevel optimization problem that searches for useful sample weights. One level concerns training the predictive model on weighted data, while the other concerns selecting the weights. In the proposed formulation, generalization complexity depends on the space of possible sample weights rather than directly on the size of the predictive model.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis in the linear setting that establishes MAPLE's insensitivity to model size. Experiments also report large improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The theory's stated scope is the linear case, while the empirical results support the broader practical motivation: controlling how training data influence learning can help address distribution shifts even when the model itself has many parameters.
icml-2022-model-agnostic-sample-reweight.tldr: MAPLE searches for training-sample weights that improve out-of-distribution generalization, with linear-case theory separating generalization complexity from model size.

paragraphs: Repeated-game learning is often studied with a fixed payoff matrix. This paper allows the matrix of a two-player zero-sum game to change over time, potentially adversarially. That makes performance harder to assess because both the rewards available to players and the game's minimax value can move during learning.

The authors use three measures: individual regret, an extended duality gap, and a new dynamic Nash equilibrium regret. The new measure tracks the cumulative difference between a player's payoff and the changing minimax game value. They develop one parameter-free algorithm with favorable guarantees for all three measures, rather than requiring a separate method for each objective.

The algorithm has two layers: a meta-algorithm learns over a collection of base learners satisfying a specified property, with additional components designed for changing games. Its guarantees adapt to different measures of payoff nonstationarity and recover the best known results when the matrix stays fixed. Empirical results further support effectiveness, while the theoretical contribution unifies several performance criteria within one adaptive learning framework.
icml-2022-no-regret-learning-in-time-var.tldr: A single parameter-free algorithm achieves adaptive guarantees under three performance measures for two-player zero-sum games with changing payoffs.

paragraphs: NysADMM solves optimization problems that combine a smooth convex loss with a convex regularizer. It builds on the inexact Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, accelerating the subproblem computations that method requires. The main device is a preconditioner constructed from a randomized low-rank Nyström approximation, which makes those computations easier to solve iteratively.

The theoretical guarantee ties the approximation rank to the effective dimension of the subproblem's regularized Gram matrix. When the rank equals that effective dimension, the subproblem can be solved in a constant number of iterations. Because much smaller ranks can work in practice, NysADMM also includes an adaptive rank-selection strategy with analogous guarantees.

Experiments on real-world datasets include lasso, logistic regression, and support vector machines. NysADMM solves these applications in half the time or less required by standard solvers in the reported evaluations. The breadth of successful applications suggests that an accelerated ADMM framework can compete across statistical learning problems often handled with specialized methods, while the constant-iteration statement specifically concerns the ADMM subproblem under the stated rank condition.
icml-2022-nysadmm-faster-composite-conve.tldr: NysADMM accelerates convex optimization using adaptive Nyström preconditioning, with strong subproblem guarantees and reported runtimes at most half those of standard solvers.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes a striking arrangement that can emerge during classification training: examples from the same class converge to identical final-layer features, while class means and classifier vectors form a highly symmetric geometric configuration. This paper investigates why that arrangement appears when training uses mean squared error loss.

Under a simplified model in which features are unconstrained, the authors characterize the entire optimization landscape. They show that every global minimizer is a neural-collapse solution and that every other critical point is a strict saddle. Such saddles have directions of negative curvature, so their local geometry differs from that of a minimum.

The paper also studies rescaled mean squared error near neural-collapse solutions and shows that adjusting the rescaling hyperparameters can improve the landscape. Experiments on practical network architectures verify the theoretical findings. The central guarantee is tied to the unconstrained-feature model; within that setting, it explains both the structure of globally optimal solutions and the geometry of all remaining critical points, giving a theoretical account of the observed collapse phenomenon.
icml-2022-on-the-optimization-landscape-.tldr: Under an unconstrained-feature model with MSE loss, neural-collapse solutions are the only global minima and every other critical point is a strict saddle.

paragraphs: Sequence modeling provides a way to learn reinforcement learning policies from previously collected data. This paper addresses the next stage: improving such a policy through new interactions with its environment. Online Decision Transformer, or ODT, brings offline pretraining and online fine-tuning into one sequence-modeling framework.

The method combines autoregressive modeling objectives with entropy regularization at the sequence level. These regularizers support exploration during online interaction, while the modeling objective maintains the sequence-based approach used for learning from existing data. The goal is to make the transition from passive data to active experience sample-efficient and to use new interactions effectively for policy improvement.

On the D4RL benchmark, ODT achieves absolute performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods and exhibits substantially larger gains during fine-tuning. Those are related but distinct findings: the final performance is competitive, and the improvement obtained through the online phase is particularly strong. The results support extending sequence-based reinforcement learning beyond offline datasets into a unified process that continues learning from task-specific environmental feedback.
icml-2022-online-decision-transformer-81.tldr: Online Decision Transformer combines offline sequence-model pretraining with entropy-regularized online learning, producing strong fine-tuning gains on D4RL.

paragraphs: A neural network can fit its training data well without generalizing equally well to new examples. This paper modifies training by adding a penalty on the norm of the loss gradient. The penalty controls how strongly the loss changes locally with the parameters, adding a geometric preference to the optimization objective.

The authors demonstrate that restricting the gradient norm can help guide optimization toward flat minima. To make the additional term practical within gradient descent, they use a first-order approximation when implementing its gradient. This connects the proposed generalization strategy to an efficient training procedure rather than leaving it solely as a property of desirable solutions.

Experiments show improved generalization across different models and datasets. The paper also establishes that sharpness-aware minimization is a special case of the proposed method, although it is not the best-performing case in the reported tasks. Better-performing choices within the method can achieve new state-of-the-art results on those tasks. The findings support gradient-norm control as a useful training mechanism, with the move toward flatter minima presented as something it can help achieve.
icml-2022-penalizing-gradient-norm-for-e.tldr: Penalizing the loss-gradient norm can guide training toward flatter minima and improve generalization through an efficient first-order implementation.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning an approximate Nash equilibrium in an episodic two-player zero-sum Markov game using only a previously collected dataset. The challenge is especially difficult when the data do not cover all policy pairs uniformly. Learning must handle distribution shift, large state spaces through function approximation, and the optimization needed to solve a game.

Pessimistic minimax value iteration, or PMVI, constructs conservative value estimates for both players to address distribution shift. It then obtains a policy pair by solving a correlated coarse equilibrium based on those estimates. The analysis gives a data-dependent upper bound on suboptimality and recovers a sublinear rate without requiring uniform dataset coverage.

An information-theoretic lower bound shows that the upper bound is nearly minimax optimal, suggesting that its data-dependent term reflects an intrinsic difficulty. The theory also identifies relative uncertainty as characterizing a necessary and sufficient condition for sample efficiency in the studied offline games. Together, these results connect achievable equilibrium-learning accuracy to the information available in the dataset, rather than imposing uniform coverage of every policy pair.
icml-2022-pessimistic-minimax-value-iter.tldr: PMVI uses pessimistic value estimates to learn approximate equilibria from offline game data, with nearly minimax-optimal guarantees without uniform coverage.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a large model by removing weights judged to be unimportant. For Transformers, those judgments are often estimated from training mini-batches, making them noisy as sampled examples and training dynamics change. A weight that appears unimportant at one moment may still be crucial, so premature removal can destabilize training and hurt generalization.

PLATON incorporates uncertainty into the importance estimate using an upper confidence bound. In particular, it tends to retain weights whose estimated importance is low but uncertain, giving their capacity more opportunity to be explored. The pruning decision therefore considers both the current importance score and how much confidence the method has in that score.

The authors evaluate PLATON with several Transformer-based models on natural language understanding, question answering, and image classification. They report notable improvements across different sparsity levels. These findings support treating uncertainty as relevant information when deciding which parameters to remove, especially when importance estimates fluctuate during training. The method's contribution is a more cautious way to interpret low estimated importance while still pursuing a smaller model.
icml-2022-platon-pruning-large-transform.tldr: PLATON improves Transformer pruning by accounting for uncertainty in weight importance, tending to retain weights whose low scores are unreliable.

paragraphs: Training labels can be imbalanced, incorrect, or influenced by human bias, making it difficult to learn a classifier that generalizes well. This paper investigates how the geometry encouraged by common classification losses can help with imperfect annotations. Its analysis examines both softmax loss and losses based on classification margins.

The authors identify maximizing the smallest sample margin as a feasible way to tighten a generalization-error bound. They then derive an optimality condition that specifies how class prototypes should be anchored. This connects the placement of class representatives to the margin of the least-separated sample, providing a theoretical motivation for controlling prototype geometry during learning.

The resulting method, prototype-anchored learning or PAL, can be incorporated into various classification schemes. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets verify its effectiveness for class-imbalanced and noise-tolerant learning. Although the motivation includes several forms of annotation imperfection, those two settings are the explicit experimental focus. The contribution links an analysis of generalization bounds to a practical method for shaping class prototypes under difficult labeling conditions.
icml-2022-prototype-anchored-learning-fo.tldr: Prototype-anchored learning uses margin-based theory to position class prototypes and improve classification with imbalanced or noisy labels.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers often convert an image into a sequence of patches. While this allows sequence-based attention to process images, it weakens the explicit representation of spatial locality: nearby patches carry visual relationships that a one-dimensional ordering does not fully express. Ripple attention is designed to bring two-dimensional spatial distance into efficient attention computation.

The method builds on kernel-based efficient attention and introduces a dynamic programming algorithm. For each query, contributions from other tokens are weighted according to their relative distances in the image plane. This makes spatial arrangement part of the attention mechanism while targeting a cost below the quadratic complexity associated with full pairwise attention.

The authors describe ripple attention as subquadratic and report linear observed runtime for the proposed computation. Experiments and analyses across visual tasks demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution is therefore both spatial and computational: it gives attention an explicit way to use image locality while retaining efficient processing. The observed linear behavior is an empirical runtime statement, distinct from the broader subquadratic characterization of the mechanism.
icml-2022-ripple-attention-for-visual-pe.tldr: Ripple attention incorporates two-dimensional spatial distance into efficient vision attention, with subquadratic complexity and observed linear runtime.

paragraphs: Invariant risk minimization aims to learn features that remain useful when the data distribution changes. This paper identifies a tension in using large networks for that goal: additional capacity can make training easier, yet its theoretical and empirical analyses show that overparameterization can make IRM particularly vulnerable to overfitting and damaged generalization.

SparseIRM addresses the tension by imposing a global sparsity constraint throughout the IRM process. The constraint limits the feature-selection budget and is intended to prevent spurious features from entering the learned solution. Applying sparsity during learning matters because removing features only after training can also discard useful invariant features.

The authors illustrate the benefit with a theoretical analysis of a simple linear case and evaluate the approach across multiple datasets and models. They report improvements over state-of-the-art methods reaching a gap of up to 29%. The findings support controlling feature selection throughout invariant learning, with the formal illustration scoped to the linear setting and the broader gains established experimentally. The largest reported gap describes the strongest observed improvement, rather than a uniform gain across settings.
icml-2022-sparse-invariant-risk-minimiza.tldr: SparseIRM constrains sparsity throughout invariant risk minimization to curb spurious feature learning and improve generalization under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization concerns using learned components in combinations beyond those previously encountered. This paper studies that ability in world models for reinforcement learning environments organized around objects. The central question is how a model of an environment can capture reusable structure that supports generalization across object compositions.

The authors give the problem an algebraic formulation, making compositional generalization something that can be analyzed explicitly. They introduce a conceptual environment called Object Library, provide two instances, and develop a principled evaluation pipeline. Within this framework, they examine methods that have exact compositional generalization and methods that lack the ability, clarifying distinctions between different modeling approaches.

The formulation also motivates a differentiable model called the Homomorphic Object-oriented World Model, or HOWM. It achieves a soft form of compositional generalization with greater efficiency, rather than the exact property considered for some of the analyzed methods. The contribution combines a formal account of the target ability, a way to measure it, and a model that makes an explicit tradeoff between exactness and efficiency.
icml-2022-toward-compositional-generaliz.tldr: An algebraic framework analyzes compositional generalization in object-based world models and motivates HOWM, a differentiable approach offering soft but more efficient generalization.
